Section 2.4 of Lock⁵ turns to the third question of data description: **how does a
quantitative variable behave across the groups defined by a categorical variable?**
For a single quantitative variable the **five-number summary** (minimum, first
quartile Q1, median, third quartile Q3, maximum) is displayed graphically as a
**boxplot**: the box spans the middle 50% of the data (its height is the
**interquartile range**, IQR = Q3 − Q1), the line inside the box marks the median,
and the whiskers reach to the most extreme values that are not flagged as
**outliers** by the 1.5 × IQR rule — any point below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above
Q3 + 1.5 × IQR is plotted as a separate dot. Boxplots reveal center, spread, skewness,
and outliers at a glance, and drawing them **side by side** for the groups of a
categorical variable (backed up by comparative means, medians, and standard
deviations) is the standard first look at a quantitative/categorical relationship.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 110–117). Skill Builders 2.153–2.162 match five-number
summaries to boxplots, read shapes and outliers off boxplots, and build boxplots
from five-number summaries; 2.163–2.172 interpret boxplots and comparative output,
including a unit built on the `HollywoodMovies` data; 2.173–2.181 examine
quantitative/categorical relationships in real datasets (`USStates`,
`BaseballHits2019`, `NutritionStudy`, `HoneybeeCircuits`, `SplitBill`,
`CollegeScores`, `HomingPigeons`); and 2.182–2.185 ask you to draw and explore
boxplots yourself. Tabs based on Lock5 data files include a small executable EDA.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
```

```{python}
#| include: false
def five_box(ax, specs, colors="#4c72b0"):
    # Draw horizontal boxplots from precomputed five-number summaries:
    # specs = [(label, min, Q1, median, Q3, max, [fliers]), ...]
    stats = [{"label": lbl, "med": med, "q1": q1, "q3": q3,
              "whislo": lo, "whishi": hi, "fliers": fl}
             for lbl, lo, q1, med, q3, hi, fl in specs]
    ax.bxp(stats, vert=False, patch_artist=True,
           boxprops=dict(facecolor=colors, alpha=0.55),
           medianprops=dict(color="black"))
    ax.set_xlabel("")
```

## Exercise 2.153

**Match each five-number summary with one of the boxplots (Q, R, S, T) in
Figure 2.38.**
*(a) (2, 12, 14, 17, 25)  (b) (5, 15, 18, 20, 23)  (c) (10, 12, 13, 18, 25)
(d) (12, 12, 15, 20, 24)*

- **(a) → S.** The box spans 12 to 17 with median 14 near its middle, and the
  values 2 and 25 fall far from the box — the plot that shows both a low and a
  high outlier, with whiskers pulled in to about 6 and 22.
- **(b) → R.** Box 15–20 with median 18 right of center and two low outliers
  near 5 (the minimum 5 lies well below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR = 15 − 7.5 = 7.5).
- **(c) → Q.** Box 12–18 with the median 13 hugging the *left* edge of the box,
  whiskers reaching 10 and 25, no outliers.
- **(d) → T.** The minimum equals Q1 (both 12), so the box begins exactly at the
  smallest value and there is *no lower whisker*; median 15, Q3 20, max 24.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Schematic boxplots of the four five-number summaries, drawn on the same scale
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.8))
five_box(ax, [
    ("(a)", 2, 12, 14, 17, 25, []),
    ("(b)", 5, 15, 18, 20, 23, []),
    ("(c)", 10, 12, 13, 18, 25, []),
    ("(d)", 12, 12, 15, 20, 24, []),
])
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.154

**Match each five-number summary with one of the boxplots (X, Y, Z, W) in
Figure 2.39.**
*(a) (1, 18, 20, 22, 25)  (b) (1, 10, 15, 20, 25)  (c) (1, 3, 5, 10, 25)
(d) (1, 1, 10, 15, 25)*

- **(a) → W.** Box sits at the right (18–22, median 20), and the minimum 1 is
  far below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR = 18 − 6 = 12, appearing as a single low outlier.
- **(b) → X.** Box 10–20 with median 15 in the middle, whiskers spanning 1 to 25,
  no outliers.
- **(c) → Y.** Box 3–10 with median 5 left of center and a single *high* outlier
  at 25 (above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 10 + 10.5 = 20.5).
- **(d) → Z.** Minimum = Q1 = 1, so the box starts right at the minimum with no
  lower whisker; box 1–15, median 10, upper whisker to 25.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Schematic boxplots of the four five-number summaries for Exercise 2.154
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.8))
five_box(ax, [
    ("(a)", 1, 18, 20, 22, 25, []),
    ("(b)", 1, 10, 15, 20, 25, []),
    ("(c)", 1, 3, 5, 10, 25, []),
    ("(d)", 1, 1, 10, 15, 25, []),
])
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.159

**Skill Builder 3 — five-number summary (210, 260, 270, 300, 320); n = 500;
tails: 210, 215, 217, 221, 225, …, 318, 319, 319, 319, 320, 320. Identify outliers
by the IQR method and draw the boxplot.**

- **No outliers.** IQR = 300 − 260 = 40, so the fences are 260 − 60 = 200 and
  300 + 60 = 360. The smallest tail value (210) is above the lower fence and the
  largest (320) is below the upper fence — nothing is flagged.
- Boxplot: box 260–300 with median 270, whiskers reaching the extremes 210 and 320.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Boxplot for Exercise 2.159, drawn from the five-number summary
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 1.8))
five_box(ax, [("2.159", 210, 260, 270, 300, 320, [])])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.160

**Skill Builder 3 — five-number summary (15, 42, 52, 56, 71); n = 120;
tails: 15, 20, 28, 30, 31, …, 64, 65, 65, 66, 71.**

- **Outliers: 15 and 20, both low.** IQR = 56 − 42 = 14, so the fences are
  42 − 21 = 21 and 56 + 21 = 77. The tail values 15 and 20 fall below 21; every
  high tail value (up to 71) is inside the upper fence.
- Boxplot: box 42–56 with median 52, lower whisker to 28 (the smallest
  non-outlier), upper whisker to 71, and dots at 15 and 20.

**Skill Builder 3 — five-number summary (42, 72, 78, 80, 99); n = 120;
tails: 42, 63, 65, 67, 68, …, 88, 89, 95, 96, 99.**

- **Outliers: 42 on the low end; 95, 96, and 99 on the high end.**

## Exercise 2.163

**Literacy Rate.** Figure 2.40 gives a boxplot of the literacy rate of the
countries of the world.

- **(a) Skewed to the left.** The left whisker is very long (down to about 50)
  and there is a cluster of low outliers (near 18, 26, and 37), while the box is
  compressed at the top of the scale near 80–96.
- **(b)** The middle half of the literacy rates lie between approximately
  **80 and 95**.
- **(c)** Five-number summary, read off the plot: approximately
  **(50, 80, 92, 96, 99)**.
- **(d) Lower.** The countries missing from the World Bank data are likely to be
  poorer, less-developed nations — precisely those with low literacy rates. If
  they were included, the low end would stretch further down and the median would
  drop below the ≈ 92 shown.

## Exercise 2.164

**Young Blood Helps Old Brains.** Old mice were randomly assigned to receive
plasma transfusions from young or old mice, and treadmill runtime (minutes) was
measured. Figure 2.41 shows side-by-side boxplots.

- **(a)** The median runtime for mice receiving **old blood is about 30 minutes**.
- **(b)** The old-blood distribution is skewed to the right (long upper tail), so
  we expect the **mean to be larger than the median** — the data give mean 34.7
  vs median 29.
- **(c)** Mice receiving **young blood** clearly ran longer — median about
  55 minutes versus about 30.
- **(d) Yes.** Runtime is associated with transfusion type: mice given young
  plasma tend to run substantially longer than mice given old plasma.
- **(e) Almost none.** The boxplots in Figure 2.41 flag no outliers in either
  group; recomputing the fences from the data, the old-blood group has one
  borderline high value (68 minutes, just above its upper fence of 67.5) and the
  young-blood group has none.

*Data:* `data/ch02/YoungBlood.csv` (n = 30), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/YoungBlood.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
yb = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/YoungBlood.csv")
yb.groupby("Plasma")["Runtime"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "min", "max"]).round(1)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Treadmill runtime in minutes for old mice receiving young or old plasma
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3))
sns.boxplot(data=yb, x="Runtime", y="Plasma", order=["Young", "Old"],
            ax=ax, color="#4c72b0", width=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Runtime (minutes)")
ax.set_ylabel("Plasma")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.165

**Football and Brain Size.** A study of n = 25 per group compared total
hippocampus volume (µL) for healthy controls, football players with no concussion
history, and football players with a history of concussions (Figure 2.42).

- **(a)** The explanatory variable — group (control / football no concussion /
  football with concussion) — is **categorical**; the response, hippocampus
  volume, is **quantitative**.
- **(b)** The **control group** has the largest volumes (median ≈ 7500) and the
  **football players with concussions** the smallest (median ≈ 5700).
- **(c)** Yes — a single **high outlier in the football-with-concussion group**,
  at about 7300 µL.
- **(d)** The third quartile for the no-concussion players is about
  **7000 µL** (upper edge of that box).
- **(e) Yes.** Median volume declines steadily from controls to non-concussed
  players to concussed players, so hippocampus size is associated with football
  experience and concussion history.
- **(f) No.** This is an observational study — nobody was assigned to play
  football or to get concussions — so confounding variables (self-selection into
  football, head impacts outside concussions, fitness, demographics) prevent a
  causal conclusion.

## Exercise 2.166

**Ronda Rousey Fight Times.** Five-number summary of her first 12 UFC fight
times, in seconds: (14, 25, 44, 64, 289). Only three fights lasted more than a
minute: 289, 267, and 66 seconds.

- **(a)** IQR = 64 − 25 = 39, so the upper fence is 64 + 1.5 × 39 = 122.5.
  **289 and 267 are high outliers** (both exceed 122.5); **66 is not** (66 < 122.5),
  it is simply the largest non-outlier.
- **(b) No low outliers.** The lower fence is 25 − 58.5 = −33.5, and no fight time
  can fall below it (minimum 14).
- **(c)** Boxplot: box 25–64 with median 44, lower whisker to 14, upper whisker
  to 66, and dots at 267 and 289.
- **(d)** The distribution is extremely skewed to the right, so the **mean is
  greater than the median** — the two huge outliers pull the mean far above 44.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Boxplot of Ronda Rousey's first 12 UFC fight times in seconds
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 1.9))
five_box(ax, [("Fight times (sec)", 14, 25, 44, 64, 66, [267, 289])])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.167

groups 1 and 2 are shown for datasets A, B, and C (Figure 2.43).

- **(a) Dataset C** shows the strongest association: the two boxes are completely
  separated (group 1 centered near 3, group 2 near 7), so knowing the group tells
  you almost exactly where a case falls.

  are essentially identical. (Dataset B is nearly as flat — its groups overlap
  heavily too — but A's groups are the most alike.)

## Exercise 2.168

**Draw Side-by-Side Boxplots.** Side-by-side boxplots that show (a) a clear
association and (b) no association between a categorical and a quantitative
variable.

- **(a)** Put the two boxes in different locations with little or no overlap —
  for example group 1 centered near 30 and group 2 near 50.
- **(b)** Make the two boxes virtually identical — same center, same spread — so
  the group label tells you nothing about the value.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Side-by-side boxplots showing a clear association versus no association
rng = np.random.default_rng(24)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3), sharey=True)
df_assoc = pd.DataFrame({"Group": ["G1", "G2"],
                         "Value": [rng.normal(30, 5, 40), rng.normal(50, 5, 40)]})
sns.boxplot(data=df_assoc.explode("Value"), x="Group", y="Value", ax=axes[0],
            color="#4c72b0", width=0.45)
axes[0].set_title("(a) Clear association", fontsize=10)
df_none = pd.DataFrame({"Group": ["G1", "G2"],
                        "Value": [rng.normal(40, 8, 40), rng.normal(40, 8, 40)]})
sns.boxplot(data=df_none.explode("Value"), x="Group", y="Value", ax=axes[1],
            color="#4c72b0", width=0.45)
axes[1].set_title("(b) No association", fontsize=10)
for a in axes:
    a.set_xlabel("Group")
    a.set_ylabel("Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.169

**How Profitable Are Hollywood Movies?** `Profitability` measures the percent of
the budget recovered in revenue; below 100 means the movie failed to cover its
budget. Figure 2.44 boxplots profitability for all 1056 movies with available
values.

- **(a) Strongly skewed to the right**, with a huge number of high outliers
  stretching from about 1000 all the way past 10,000 (the largest,
  *The Devil Inside*, had a tiny budget and relatively high gross revenue).
- **(b)** The range is roughly **10,000**: the smallest profitability is about 0–2
  and the largest outlier is about 10,200. (The data give max − min =
  10176 − 2 ≈ 10,174.)
- **(c)** The median is hard to read on the compressed scale but is about
  **250–300** (the data give 269): half the movies recovered less than about
  2.7 times their budget — and half recovered more.
- **(d)** The **mean is greater than the median** — the many extreme high
  outliers pull the mean far to the right of the median.

*Data:* `data/ch02/HollywoodMovies.csv` (n = 1295 rows; 1056 with profitability
values), downloaded from <https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HollywoodMovies.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
hm = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/HollywoodMovies.csv")
prof = hm["Profitability"].dropna()
print(prof.agg(["count", "min", "median", "max"]).round(0).to_string())
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Profitability of Hollywood movies, 2012 to 2018
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.6))
sns.boxplot(x=prof, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0", width=0.4)
ax.set_xlabel("Profitability (percent of budget recovered)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.170

**Audience Scores on Rotten Tomatoes.** Five-number summary of `AudienceScore`:
(10, 49, 64, 77, 99). Any outliers by the IQR method? How low would an average
score have to be to qualify as a low outlier?

- **No outliers.** IQR = 77 − 49 = 28, so the fences are 49 − 42 = 7 and
  77 + 42 = 119. The minimum (10) is above the lower fence and the maximum (99)
  is below the upper fence — nothing is flagged.
- An average audience score would have to fall **below 7** on the 0–100 scale to
  qualify as a low outlier — an almost universally panned movie.

```{python}
#| echo: false
hm["AudienceScore"].quantile([0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]).to_frame("AudienceScore").T
```

## Exercise 2.171

**Do Movie Budgets Differ Based on the Genre of the Movie?** Side-by-side
boxplots of `Budget` (millions of dollars) by `Genre` for 2018 movies —
Action, Comedy, Drama, and Horror (Figure 2.45).

- **(a) Action** movies clearly have the largest budgets (median about \$90
  million, reaching \$300 million); **Horror** movies have the smallest
  (median about \$10–25 million).
- **(b) Action** has by far the biggest spread (IQR from roughly 35 to 150);
  **Horror** has the smallest spread, with all its budgets packed below about
  \$50 million.
- **(c) Yes.** The budget distributions differ markedly from genre to genre —
  action budgets sit far above the others — so knowing a movie's genre conveys
  real information about its budget; the two variables are associated.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Movie budgets in millions of dollars by genre for 2018 movies
h18 = hm[(hm["Year"] == 2018) & hm["Genre"].isin(["Action", "Comedy", "Drama", "Horror"])]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
sns.boxplot(data=h18, x="Budget", y="Genre",
            order=["Action", "Comedy", "Drama", "Horror"],
            ax=ax, color="#4c72b0", width=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Budget (millions of dollars)")
ax.set_ylabel("Genre")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.174

**Hits in Baseball.** Are total team hits different between the American League
and National League? Figure 2.47 shows side-by-side boxplots of team hits
(`BaseballHits2019`).

- **(a)** Median hits: AL ≈ 1380 and NL ≈ 1380 — the two medians are nearly
  identical (the data give 1379 vs 1378), so there is **not much difference in
  median hits** between the leagues.
- **(b)** The **AL is more variable** (standard deviation ≈ 86 vs ≈ 67), with both
  a higher maximum (1554 vs 1502) and a lower minimum (1299 vs 1281); the NL
  teams are packed more tightly. The AL average is also slightly higher
  (mean 1410 vs 1392), pulled up by a few high-hitting teams.

*Data:* `data/ch02/BaseballHits2019.csv` (n = 30 teams), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/BaseballHits2019.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
bb = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/BaseballHits2019.csv")
bb.groupby("League")["Hits"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std", "min", "max"]).round(1)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Team hits in the 2019 season by league
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
sns.boxplot(data=bb, x="League", y="Hits", order=["AL", "NL"],
            ax=ax, color="#4c72b0", width=0.45)
ax.set_xlabel("League")
```

## Exercise 2.176

**How Do Honeybees Communicate Quality?** Scouts waggle-dance to describe
candidate homes; scientists counted circuits for the 41 scouts describing a
high-quality option and the 37 describing a low-quality option
(`HoneybeeCircuits`).

- **(a) Yes.** Scouts describing the **high-quality** site perform far more
  circuits (median ≈ 80) than those describing the **low-quality** site (median
  of 0 — most barely dance at all): the dance length advertises site quality.
- **(b)** *High:* five-number summary (0, 7.5, 80, 122.5, 440), IQR = 115, upper
  fence = 122.5 + 172.5 = **295** → the values **330 and 440 are high outliers**.
  *Low:* (0, 0, 0, 42.5, 185), IQR = 42.5, upper fence = 42.5 + 63.75 =
  **106.25** → **140, 175, and 185 are high outliers**. Neither group has any low
  outliers (all values ≥ 0 and the lower fences are negative).
- **(c)** $\bar{x}_H - \bar{x}_L = 90.5 - 30.0 = \mathbf{60.5}$ circuits.
- **(d)** z-scores for the largest values: high group
  $(440 - 90.5)/94.6 \approx \mathbf{3.69}$; low group
  $(185 - 30.0)/49.4 \approx \mathbf{3.14}$. The **high-quality group's maximum is
  more extreme relative to its group**.
- **(e) No** — the 95% rule is for roughly bell-shaped data, and both
  distributions are strongly right-skewed (piled up at 0 with long right tails),
  so about 95% of the data does *not* fall within two standard deviations of the
  mean here.

*Data:* `data/ch02/HoneybeeCircuits.csv` (n = 78), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HoneybeeCircuits.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
hc = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/HoneybeeCircuits.csv")
rows = []
for q, g in hc.groupby("Quality"):
    s = g["Circuits"]
    q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
    hi = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
    rows.append({"Quality": q, "n": len(s), "mean": round(s.mean(), 1),
                 "sd": round(s.std(), 1), "upper fence": round(hi, 1),
                 "high outliers": sorted(s[s > hi].tolist())})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Number of waggle-dance circuits by quality of the described site
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
sns.stripplot(data=hc, x="Circuits", y="Quality", order=["Low", "High"],
              ax=ax, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.6, size=4)
ax.set_xlabel("Circuits in waggle dance")
ax.set_ylabel("Site quality")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.177

**Split the Bill?** 48 Israeli college students ate in groups of six; before

- **(a) Numerical summary:** students told to **split** the bill spent
  substantially more on average — mean 50.92 ILS vs 37.29 ILS for those paying
